subject: mathematics
question_text: If f: A→B is a function and I_A, I_B are identity functions on A, B respectively then prove that foI_A = f = I_Bof.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.15 — LAQ chapter 1 Functions, question 3. The 3+4 split is printed in that book's margin; the only appearance year printed is AP 18. Publisher's claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Written lines use render:'katex' wherever the identity functions appear, because a capital-letter subscript has no Unicode form (docs/IPE_MATHS_1A_SOURCE.md). Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Proof that foI_A = f.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove that composing f with the identity on either side leaves f unchanged — the two parts, and how each part goes.

steps.label: Write what is given
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Write down what each identity function does before you use it — the whole proof is one line of algebra once that is on the page.
steps.memory_tip: Write what each identity DOES to an element first; the proof is one line of algebra after that.

lines.text: I_A : A \to A, \quad I_B : B \to B
\text{To prove: } f \circ I_A = f = I_B \circ f

recall.must_convey: That the identity on A sends every element of A to itself, and the identity on B does the same on B. If only the name 'identity function' is spoken with no statement of what it does, confidence 0.5 or lower.
accept: the identity on A sends every a to itself and the identity on B sends every b to itself
I A of a equals a and I B of b equals b
given f from A to B and the two identity functions which leave every element unchanged
identity function ante prathi element ni ade return chestundi
we have f and the identities on A and on B that fix every element
reject: I A and I B are identities

steps.why: Both halves of this proof are the single fact that an identity function changes nothing. Writing that fact down first turns the rest into one substitution.
common_mistakes: Naming the identity function without saying what it does to an element.
Mixing up which identity acts on A and which on B.

steps.label: Identity on the right
steps.margin_note: Four of the eight marks. Two things earn them: that both sides have domain A, and the one-line substitution. Do not skip the domain line.
steps.memory_tip: The inner function must accept elements of A, so it is I_A. Do not skip the domain line.

lines.text: I_A : A \to A \text{ and } f : A \to B
So both sides have the same domain A.

recall.must_convey: That f o I_A maps A to B like f does, and that applying it to a gives f of I_A of a, which is f of a because the identity leaves a alone.
accept: f composed with I A goes from A to B same as f then f of I A of a is f of a because I A of a is a
apply it to a the identity gives back a so you get f of a hence the composition equals f
both have domain A and the value is f of a so they are the same function
I A of a equals a kabatti f of a vasthundi so f o I A equals f
the identity on the inside does nothing so the composition is just f
reject: the identity does nothing so it is equal

steps.why: The identity sits on the input side here, so it acts first and hands a straight back to f. Nothing about f is used except that it is a function.
common_mistakes: Proving only the values match and never the domains.
Writing I_B where I_A belongs — the inner function must accept elements of A.

steps.label: Identity on the left
steps.margin_note: Four of the eight marks. Same shape as part (i), but the identity now acts on the OUTPUT, so it is I_B and it uses I_B(b) = b.
steps.memory_tip: Here the identity acts on the OUTPUT, so it is I_B and uses I_B(b) = b. Write it out, not 'by symmetry'.

lines.text: f : A \to B \text{ and } I_B : B \to B
So both sides have the same domain A.

recall.must_convey: That I_B o f also maps A to B, and applying it to a gives I_B of f(a), which is f(a) because the identity on B leaves f(a) alone. The identity must be I_B here, acting after f.
accept: I B composed with f goes from A to B and I B of f of a is f of a because I B fixes every element of B
here the identity acts after f so it takes f of a and returns f of a
f of a is in B and the identity on B leaves it alone so the composition is f
f of a B lo untundi so I B daanini marchadu hence equal
same argument on the other side with I B instead of I A

steps.why: Here the identity acts on the output, which lives in B — that is why it must be I_B and not I_A. The two parts are not the same statement; they are the two sides of the composition.
common_mistakes: Writing 'by symmetry' instead of doing the second part — the examiner marks it separately.
Using I_A on the output side, where the elements are f(a) ∈ B.
Dropping the domain line in part (ii) after writing it in part (i).

steps.label: Conclude
steps.margin_note: No separate mark. Write the double equality exactly as the question stated it.
steps.memory_tip: Write the DOUBLE equality exactly as the question stated it.

recall.must_convey: That both compositions equal f, stated as the single double equality the question asked for.
accept: f composed with I A equals f equals I B composed with f
both compositions give f so the double equality holds
hence f o I A equals f equals I B o f
rendu vaipula identity vaadina f ye vastundi
the identity on either side leaves f unchanged

steps.why: The question asked for a chain of two equalities. Writing it as one line shows both halves were proved, not just one.
common_mistakes: Writing only one of the two equalities in the final line.
